title: Banks splash $30m in executive buyouts
full_text:
The country's four major banks have agreed to pay nearly $30 million in forgone bonuses and shares to poach finance and technology executives from rivals, amid an intense battle for talent over the last year.
Bank disclosures reveal the four companies have promised $29.4 million to lure recruits in the financial year just ended, often to replace a new executive's former incentives as is common practice on Wall Street.
Called buyouts, the incentives are usually portioned over several years rather than paid on signing and are only counted in pay disclosures as they vest. Last year's deal flurry looks unprecedented, worth three times the $9.7 million of buyouts agreed to in the previous four combined.
The record was driven by two marquee hires during what was an extraordinary poaching wave last year, as three relatively new chief executives worked hard to reshape their leadership teams.
Westpac's chief financial officer Nathan Goonan was hired from the same job at National Australia Bank. Westpac covered $7.83 million of the $9.47 million in incentives he left behind. He still took $2.37 million of shares and $463,000 in deferred bonuses from NAB, before moving to Westpac on roughly the same $3.9 million-a-year pay.
The bigger one was Inder Singh, who NAB signed as chief financial officer and group executive for strategy on a $10 million deal from QBE Insurance. His buyout was valued between $9.05 million, as the rights were accounted by QBE, and the $12.3 million they would have been worth once fully vested.
Singh is also expected to have forgone a bonus of almost $2 million the year before. His new $5.4 million annual package is about the same as his old one.
His signing pushed NAB to the top of the buyout board. The bank also paid $4.67 million to pry its top artificial intelligence and digital executive Pete Steel from British lender Lloyds.
NAB chief executive Andrew Irvine noted the bank's "deliberate executive talent development and succession planning" as a critical part of his strategy, as Steel and transformation executive Shane Conway absorbed the portfolios of departing executives Les Matheson and Patrick Wright.
Westpac agreed to pay $3.79 million for Macquarie's banking and financial services chief information officer Richard Heeley, who joined in August.
ANZ chief executive Nuno Matos wooed his new chief operating officer Stephen White from Santander with a $6.4 million buyout. The bank agreed to another $500,000 for its new retail boss Pedro Rodeia, who left his role as a senior partner at global consultancy McKinsey.
Suzanne Wohlthat, principal at remuneration and governance advisory Guerdon Associates, said growth in long-term incentives was helping drive higher buyouts.
"The market recognises this as the price of hiring a strong candidate from outside the company. It also gives the incoming executive immediate 'skin in the game'," Wohlthat said, adding investors and proxy advisers preferred deferred equity to cash.
"Whether the company buying out the executive adheres to this preference depends on negotiations, administrative complexity, whether the original incentives were in equity or cash, and when they were scheduled to be paid." The flurry of appointments overshadowed the previous year's buyouts, which in turn were bigger than the previous three 12-month periods.
Prior period deals included $2.88 million for Westpac's business bank boss Paul Fowler and $2.24 million for chief people officer Kate Dee's forgone incentives. NAB business bank boss Andrew Auerbach got a $1.6 million entitlement in the same year, following Irvine from the Bank of Montreal.
Banks must only publicly disclose the pay of key management personnel, meaning the detail of any other likely packages are not provided to the market. Andrew McMullan, who Westpac signed from CBA as chief data, digital and AI officer, slipped below the radar.
